Through that span sage rulers succeeded one another and crises arose in turn; never once did a dynasty survive without entrusting power to worthy men, keeping upright counselors near, and thereby renewing its glory. Neglect it for a single day and the great vessel is overturned — the shame of the ancestral temple becomes an eternal regret. I respectfully cite the Spring and Autumn Annals: the ruler's way lies in embodying the origin and holding the correct position — Dong Zhongshu explained this to Emperor Wu of Han long ago. What he left unsaid, I may now set forth fully for Your Majesty. When a ruler succeeds his predecessor, the accession must be recorded — to set the beginning right; At the end one must record where he died — to set the ending right. Therefore a ruler must speak upright words, walk the upright path, occupy the rightful place, and keep upright men near. I further cite the Spring and Autumn Annals: "The gate commander assassinated Prince Yu of Wu," and does not record him as ruler. The Annals rebukes him for keeping worthy men at a distance and drawing near to executioners — he had ceased to be a true ruler. I humbly urge Your Majesty to reflect on the founding ancestors' toil and heed the Annals' warning on succession. To clarify the foundations of law and order, speak upright words and walk the upright path; To choke off the drift toward regicide, hold the throne in dignity and keep honest men close. Banish the butcher's minions; cherish the blunt counselors who speak truth; let your chief ministers govern, and let every office do its work. How can five or six favored intimates run the empire — issuing Your Majesty's orders in name while seizing your power in fact, awing the court and dominating the realm, so that no minister dares speak and the Son of Heaven cannot control them? Disaster is ripening behind the palace walls; treachery is breeding within the curtained hall. I fear that Cao Jie and Hou Lan live again in our time — this is why the inner palace is on the verge of upheaval. I respectfully cite the Spring and Autumn Annals: in Duke Ding of Lu's first year, spring is recorded but the first month is not — because the former ruler could not end his reign properly, the successor could not begin his properly; hence the Annals says Duke Ding had no legitimate beginning. Today loyal ministers have nowhere to place their trust; eunuch commanders hold the power to make and unmake emperors. They prevented your predecessor from ending his reign in peace and have kept you from beginning yours in legitimacy. Moreover no crown heir has been appointed, the suburban sacrifices have not been performed, the roles of generals and ministers remain unsettled, and rank and title are in confusion — this is why the altars of state are in danger. I respectfully cite the Spring and Autumn Annals: "Wang Zhaozi killed the Earl of Shao and the Earl of Mao" The Annals' principle is that mutual killings between equals are not recorded. Yet this case is recorded — to emphasize his usurpation of the royal command. What Heaven bestows rests with the ruler; what the ruler bestows rests with his command. One who holds the command yet loses it is no ruler; One who encroaches on the command and monopolizes it is no minister. When ruler and minister no longer act as they should, the realm is about to topple — this is why. I respectfully cite the Spring and Autumn Annals: Zhao Yang of Jin led the troops of Jinyang in rebellion against the state. Today sovereign power erodes daily, while the military commissioners grow insolent on their borders. Some who know nothing of a subject's duty take the lead in rebellion in the name of saving the throne; Without heeding the Annals' subtle warnings, those who raise armies claim righteousness in driving out evil. Then government and punishment no longer come from the throne, and war begins with the regional lords — this is why turmoil is about to engulf the empire. Fan Kuai burst through the door in tears; Yuan Ang blocked the carriage with bold remonstrance; Jing Fang spoke in righteous anger and lost his life; Dou Wu ignored all danger and died for his cause — Your Majesty knows all this well. I respectfully cite the Spring and Autumn Annals: Hu Shegu of Jin killed Yang Chufu. Duke Xiang failed to secure the hidden levers of power, and Chufu met a violent death — for this the Annals rebukes him. When the ruler reveals his mind, those below dare not speak their full mind; When the ruler leaks what is said to him, those below dare not speak freely. The Commentary speaks of "approaching the knee" and "deceptive words"; the Changes has the warnings "sacrificing one's life" and "ruining success." Today's chief ministers are not unable to speak — they fear Your Majesty will not act on what they say. If Your Majesty ignores their counsel, you will inevitably leak what they say; If ministers speak and nothing is done, they will surely suffer for it. This only silences upright ministers and strengthens wicked ones. Therefore if they wish to speak fully, they fear for their lives; If they wish to speak their full mind, they fear ruining what good might yet be done. So they hesitate and hold back, waiting for Your Majesty to understand — only then will they offer their full counsel. Why not, between sessions of court, from time to time enter the informal hall, summon the worthy chancellors and venerable ministers of the day, and ask their plans for holding off disaster and restoring order? Block the paths of hidden evil; remove favored intimates; restrain those who encroach and coerce; restore the work of purging faction; warn against what must be warned against; worry over what must be worried over. If you could not set things right before, set them right now; If you could not set the beginning right, set the ending right. Then you may reverently uphold the canonical models, fully inherit the great enterprise, achieve the fruits of employing worthy men, and be free of the worry of toiling past dusk. What I said earlier — "To follow the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors and restore the ancestors' legacy, take as mirror the rise and fall of former ages and learn from present success and failure" — I have heard that Yao and Shun brought order to the realm because they could appoint the nine ministers, the four mountain lords, and the twelve pasture lords — making the right appointments, assigning clear duties, and never encroaching on their offices. Offices went to the capable; the ruler's circle to the worthy. Yi Yin and Yu Ya stood below, yet though humble they were surely elevated; The Four Evils sat at court, yet though powerful they were surely punished. Weigh safety against danger; know what to embrace and what to reject. Down to the two generations of Qin and the Yuan and Cheng reigns of Han — all wished to govern like Yao and Shun, yet in the end perished because they failed to see the pivot of safety and danger, did not know what to embrace and reject, did not entrust great ministers, did not distinguish the wicked, did not keep loyal men near, and did not banish slanderers. I humbly urge Your Majesty to examine why Yao and Shun rose, and take that as your bright model; Take as mirror why Qin and Han fell, and be warned and vigilant hereafter. Do not say that the court lacks worthy chancellors or that the offices lack worthy men. The statutes are not yet broken and the laws still stand — who would not wish to serve as your minister and bring peace to the age? Why does Your Majesty neglect them? And there are men in office beyond their ability and at your side though unworthy — wicked as the Four Evils, deceitful as Zhao Gao, treacherous as Gong Yu and Shi Xian — why should Your Majesty hesitate to remove them? The throne has its rightful holder; Heaven's mandate its proper allotment; the ancestral temple its numinous power; loyal ministers their steadfast hearts — Your Majesty, remember this! Qin perished through excessive harshness; Han perished through excessive weakness. Harshness drives wicked ministers to kill their ruler from fear of death; weakness lets treacherous ministers steal power and intimidate the throne. I observe that Emperor Jingzong did not guard against Qin's disaster and did not cut off its first shoots; I humbly urge Your Majesty to deeply heed the lesson of Han's fall and stop the drift while it can still be stopped. Then the ancestors' great enterprise may be renewed and the distant example of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors may be pursued. What I said earlier — "Your Majesty's mind has not reached every truth; below, the people's feelings are blocked and cannot reach you; Your conduct has not won full trust; above, your grace is dammed and cannot reach the people below." — Moreover the people's suffering in misery — Your Majesty has no way to know it; Then though Your Majesty has a parent's heart for the people, they have no way to believe it. I respectfully cite the Spring and Autumn Annals' record of "Liang perished," and does not record "was taken" — Liang destroyed itself because its rulers' minds were clouded and their ears and eyes blocked; wicked policies issued from above, men became bandits below, and none knew why — and so brought ruin on themselves. I have heard that a ruler is honored because he gives weight to the altars of state; The altars are weighty because the people are preserved. If the people are not preserved, the altars cannot hold their weight; If the altars lose their weight, the ruler cannot preserve his honor. Therefore to govern the realm one must know the people's condition. The people are Your Majesty's own children. Your Majesty ought to have the benevolent nurture them personally — as protector and tutor, as nurse and feeder, as teacher and guide. When people trust their ruler, they revere him as a spirit and love him as a parent. Today it is not so. Your Majesty keeps favored intimates near; they are assigned to offices by department; clerks and clients are summoned and installed; relying on their bribes, you lend them your authority. The greater ones command military regions; the lesser ones serve as prefects and governors. In high office they offer no pure and generous government. Only the harm of gluttonous greed; In low office they show no loyal integrity, only treachery and fraud. Therefore the people fear their rulers like wolves and jackals and hate them like sworn enemies. Now the empire is destitute; people scatter everywhere; the hungry cannot eat, the cold cannot be clothed, widows and orphans cannot survive, and the old, young, and sick cannot be cared for. Moreover the state's power rests solely with those at your side; greedy ministers extort wealth to secure favor, and corrupt clerks manipulate the law for their own ends. Cries of injustice reach up to heaven and down to the underworld; ghosts and spirits seethe with anger, and yin and yang fall out of balance. The ruler's gate is ten thousand li away and grievances cannot be heard; scholars have nowhere to turn, and the people have nowhere to place their trust. Officials are corrupt and the people impoverished; bandits rise on every side; the state is crumbling — disaster may come at any moment. If plague and famine follow, I fear Chen Sheng and Wu Guang will rise again — not only in Qin — and the Red Eyebrows and Yellow Turbans — not only in Han. That is why I beat my breast in anguish and weep blood for Your Majesty. If this is so, the people suffer in misery — how can Your Majesty know it? Your Majesty has a parent's heart for the people — how can they believe it? This is exactly what makes true your own words — "Your conduct has not won full trust; your mind has not reached every truth" — and no wonder. I have heard that when Emperor Yuan of Han first took the throne, he reformed more than seventy institutions; his heart was sincere and his reputation splendid. Yet the statutes grew daily disordered, the dynasty daily declined, wickedness daily strengthened, and the people daily distressed — because he could not select worthy men and employ them, and lost hold of the helm. Since Your Majesty has held the realm, you have toiled in worry and diligence for the myriad masses, repeatedly issuing virtuous pronouncements; throughout the four seas none failed to raise their heads and sigh with relief, rejoicing that they were reborn from among the dead. I beg Your Majesty to be careful at the end as at the beginning, to satisfy the hopes of all under Heaven. If you can truly return state authority to the chancellor and military authority to the generals, remove the government of greedy ministers gathering levies, eliminate the harm of treacherous officials seizing opportunities, draw near only the loyal and worthy and employ only the upright — hear none of the words of inner favorites and convenient flatterers. Select officials who are clear and cautious, choose leaders who are benevolent and gracious, quicken them with benefit, warm them with benevolence, teach them filial piety and kindness, guide them with virtue and righteousness, remove the blockage of ears and eyes, connect the feelings of above and below — then make the ten thousand states joyful and at peace and the myriad masses revive and rest; then what you intend will reach everywhere and what you enact will win trust everywhere. What I said earlier — "if you wish the myriad masses to be transformed, cultivate yourself first to lead them" — I have heard: virtue is for cultivating the self, teaching is for guiding others; cultivate it, then men without exhortation come of themselves; guide it, then men earnestly act and broadly follow. Therefore the noble man wishes government to be carried out, and so he takes the lead with his own person; wishes men to follow transformation, and so he governs them with the Way. Now you take the lead with your person yet government is not necessarily carried out, govern with the Way yet men have not followed transformation — is it that the aim of establishing teaching has not exhausted its methods? The method of establishing teaching lies in the ruler clearly regulating it and the minister loyally carrying it out; the ruler takes knowing men as clarity, the minister takes correcting the times as loyalty; knowing men lies in employing the worthy and removing the perverse, correcting the times lies in securing the foundation and keeping to the law. If the worthy are not employed, heavy rewards are insufficient to encourage good; if the perverse are not removed, severe punishments are insufficient to prohibit wrong; if the foundation is not secure, people scatter; if the law is not kept, government disperses — yet wishing teaching to arrive and transformation to be carried out cannot be obtained. If you can repel treacherous perversity without favoring those at your side, raise the worthy and upright without neglecting the distant — then transformation will soak the court; love others and enrich the foundation, divide duties and keep to the law, cultivate yourself and extend to others, begin within and accomplish without — then transformation will travel the realm. What I said earlier — "if you wish the vital energies to harmonize, follow their nature to guide them" — one should bring the people into benevolence and longevity. If one wishes the people benevolent and long-lived, it lies in establishing institutions and cultivating transformation. When institutions are established, expenditures are economized; when expenditures are economized, levies are light; when levies are light, the people grow wealthy; when transformation is cultivated, contention ceases; when contention ceases, punishments are clear; when punishments are clear, the people are at peace. once wealthy, then benevolence and righteousness arise; once at peace, then longevity arrives. Hearts of benevolence and longevity are moved below, qi of peace and harmony respond above — therefore disasters do not arise, auspicious omens arrive in succession, the four directions reach tranquility, and the ten thousand things all succeed. What I said earlier — "relieving drought and famine lies in attaining utmost sincerity" — I respectfully examine the Spring and Autumn Annals: within the seventh month of Duke Xi of Lu, "no rain" is recorded three times — because that ruler had a mind to care for the people; across three years of Duke Wen, it is recorded only once — because that ruler had no heart of compassion for the people. Therefore when Xi attained sincerity, drought did not harm the crops; when Wen lacked care and compassion, drought became true disaster. If Your Majesty truly has a heart to care for the people, there will be no change that becomes disaster. What I said earlier — "broad sowing and planting depend on observing the people's capacity to produce food" — I respectfully examine the Spring and Autumn Annals: "A ruler must constantly observe what the people labor at. When the people labor at physical strength, public works grow scarce; when they labor at wealth, tribute and levies shrink; when they labor at securing food, the hundred affairs are abandoned." Today wealth, food, and strength are all overstrained. I beg Your Majesty to set aside the toil of the hundred affairs and broaden the work of the three farming seasons — then sowing and planting will not fail. What I said earlier — "the state's granaries hold little because redundant consumption remains excessive" — I respectfully examine the Spring and Autumn Annals: "Zangsun Chen requested grain from Qi." The Annals condemn him for lacking nine years' stores — one year of poor harvest and the common people went hungry. I beg to expel idle wanderers to deepen farming, cut non-urgent expenditures to nourish the people — then granary stores will not run dry. What I said earlier — "the officials' paths multiplying, rooted in wrongful selection and appointment" — this is because the state does not draw on men's full talents, and appointments do not clarify what truly matters. Today in appointing men, Your Majesty seeks reputation but not substance; therefore those who advance attend to show but not to substance. I beg to examine the substance of performance evaluations and fix the system of advancement — then the multiplied paths of officials will subside. What I said earlier — "the powerful and cunning overstepping bounds because inner and outer law differ" — because official prohibitions are not one. I respectfully examine the Spring and Autumn Annals: when Duke Huan of Qi covenanted with the feudal lords, dates were usually omitted; yet the covenant at Kuiqiu is specially dated — praising his ability to proclaim the Son of Heaven's prohibitions and lead the states in keeping to the royal laws; therefore the Annals record it in full. Offices were what the Five Emperors and Three Kings established; laws were what Gaozu and Taizong enacted. Laws should be unified; offices should have correct titles. Now again outer and inner officials are divided in posts, and Southern Bureau and Northern Bureau offices are established — violate a prohibition in the south and flee to the north; be punished outside and break the law within; laws issue from many gates and men have nowhere to turn — truly because military and agricultural power diverge, and inner and outer law are separate. I have heard that in antiquity the well-field system regulated military levies, agricultural seasons were interwoven with military training, fiefs were tallied for chariot and foot numbers, and commanders were appointed from among the chief ministers — thus military and agriculture were one, civil and martial shared one direction, to secure the state and check rebellion. When Emperor Taizong first established the dynastic institutions, he also established the fubing militia; Terrace offices and army guards, civil and martial jointly administered; in peaceful years they sheathed bows and labored in the fields; when trouble arose they set aside plows and took up arms — thereby restoring the ancient system without abandoning the old institutions. Now it is not so. the Minister of War does not know the military registers, and attends court only as a formality; the Six Armies do not preside over military affairs, and exist only to nurture ranks and honors. Military affairs are merged with inner eunuch government; military regulations are attached to inner attendants' offices. One head dons the military cap and hates civil officials like sworn enemies; one foot steps through the army gate and regards farmers as nothing. Their stratagems are insufficient to cut down treacherous rebels, yet their cunning suffices to raise and lower authority and favor; their courage is insufficient to guard the altars of state, yet their violence suffices to prey on lanes and hamlets. They bind feudal ministers, overawe chief ministers, shatter the royal measure, and muddy the constants of court governance. They display the might of warriors to control the ruler and father above; they borrow the Son of Heaven's command to repel heroes below. They harbor treachery and watch for openings, but have no principle of bowing to duty and dying in hardship. Is this the purpose of the former kings in weaving civil and martial together! I beg Your Majesty to thread civil and martial Ways together, equalize military and agricultural achievement, correct titles of noble and base, unify inner and outer law, select army guards' duties, and repair the provincial offices; near at hand honor the regulations of the Zhenguan reign, far off restore the institutions of the accomplished Zhou: from the capital domain discipline the subordinate states, from the Son of Heaven down to the feudal lords — then you can restrain the strong among overbearing and cunning men, and there will be no calamity of overstepping bounds. What I said earlier — "students growing idle because school offices are abandoned" — broadly the state values their stipends and despises their ability, puts position before conduct; therefore the myriad offices lack mastery of the classics, and students have no heart to cultivate their studies. What I said earlier — "the commanderies interfering with prohibitions because the wrong men are appointed" — I hold that the post of regional inspector is where the root of order and disorder lies and where the court's laws and institutions reside; with authority one can repel overbearing strongmen, with kindness benefit orphans and widows, with strength repel treacherous bandits, and with government shift customs and mores. As for commanders and officers who have seen battle, and the sons and younger brothers of meritorious ministers — each asks to be rewarded as appropriate. If one lacks the art of governing men, he should not hold this office — then the calamity of interfering with prohibitions will end. What I said earlier — "the hundred crafts growing excessive in cleverness because institutions are not established" — I ask to regulate implements, vehicles, and dress by office rank and stipend grade, and prohibit gold, silver, pearls, jade, brocade, embroidery, and carving and inlay from being hoarded in private chambers — then there will be no cleverness that unsettles the heart. What I said earlier — "distinguishing branches and leaves" — this is because examining words inquires into conduct. What I said earlier — "taking form in shame and regulation" — this is because guiding through virtue aligns ritual. What I said earlier — "reflecting that producers are few and consumers many, and that idle wanderers may be dismissed" — has already been set forth above. What I said earlier — "orders being numerous yet governance rare, and that the essential is to examine whether they are carried out" — I have heard that commands are the instruments of governing the state: the ruler examines and issues them, ministers receive and carry them out — to violate the superior intent is an unpardonable crime. Today Your Majesty's orders are numerous yet governance is rare — can it be that those who hold them conceal and deceive? What I said earlier — "broadly gather worthy men, and I beg Your Majesty to accept their words; come to court and await inquiry — then would this petty official dare cherish his life" — I have heard that Chao Cuo drew up the plan to reduce the feudal lords for Han — it was not that he did not know disaster was coming. The loyal minister's heart, the stalwart's integrity: if it profits the altars of state, death brings no regret. Now I am not unaware that when words issue disaster follows, and when plans are carried out the body is punished — I grieve the altars' peril and mourn the people's suffering: how could I bear to temporize with the times' taboos and steal one life of Your Majesty's favor! Formerly Long Feng died and Shang was awakened; Bi Gan died and Zhou was awakened; Han Fei died and Han was awakened; Chen Fan died and Wei was awakened. Now in my coming, the responsible offices perhaps dare not recommend my words; Your Majesty again has no means to discern my heart — on retiring I will surely be executed at the hands of powerful ministers. I would be fortunate to follow the Four in the underworld — that is indeed my wish. What I do not know is: when I am killed, after my death, who will awaken them? As for the ruler's faults, the flaws in government and teaching, and the abuses of former days — I have already spoken of them. As for spreading benefit to the lower lands, cultivating governance like that of near antiquity, and attaining peace — it lies in Your Majesty's carrying it out, nothing more. Yet what was set forth above was truly because I personally received the sage inquiry — how could I not respond item by item. Though I am foolish, I hold that it has not reached the great beginning of transformation and teaching, the essential Way of the august kings. I beg Your Majesty to serve Heaven and Earth to teach reverence, attend the ancestral temples to teach filial piety, nurture the aged to teach respect for elders, cherish the people to teach kindness to the young, harmonize the vital energies to warm and nurture, fan the great harmony toward benevolence and longevity — then you may roam free in non-action, fold your arms, and let transformation be accomplished. As for reflecting on the potter's wheel — it lies in selecting chief ministers to entrust with it, letting them wield the handle of creation and transformation; reflecting on securing and stabilizing the realm — it lies in selecting generals and commanders to entrust with it, letting them fulfill the trust outside the frontier passes; reflecting on the hundred measures' lack of correctness — it lies in selecting the myriad offices to entrust with it, letting them focus on keeping to their professional duties; reflecting on the people's grievance and pain — it lies in selecting good local officials to entrust with it, letting them clarify the arts of kindness and nurturing. Then naturally your words suffice to teach the realm, your conduct suffices to model it, your benevolence suffices to encourage good, your righteousness suffices to prohibit wrong — why must you rise at midnight and dine at dusk, toil your spirit and be ever vigilant, only then attain governance! That year Left Regular Attendant of the Cavalry Feng Su, Vice Minister of Rites Jia Su, and Bureau Director of the Storehouses Pang Yan served as examination graders for the policy essays; the three were literary men of the time. Seeing Liu Fen's itemized answers, they sighed in admiration and lamentation, holding them to surpass the ancient Chao Cuo and Dong Zhongshu. The discourse was incisive and impassioned, and the scholar community was deeply moved. At the time twenty-two passed the examination, but inner eunuchs held power and the examiners dared not keep Liu Fen on the roster; public opinion clamored in outrage. Upright men who kept to the Way circulated his text, and some wept face to face as they read it. Remonstrating officials and investigating censors clenched their wrists in indignation, but the ministers in power smoothed matters over to avoid the yellow gate's resentment. Only Li He, who had passed the examination, said to others: "Liu Fen did not place, yet our cohort passed — how thick is our face indeed." He asked to yield the office he had received to Fen; though the matter was not granted, scholars praised him. Linghu Chu was at Xingyuan and Niu Sengru was stationed at Xiangyang; each recruited Liu Fen as a staff member and treated him like a teacher or friend. He ended his career as censor on a military commissioner's staff. Li Shangyin, whose courtesy name was Yishan, came from Henei in Huai prefecture. His great-grandfather Shuhuan passed the jinshi examination at nineteen and ended his career as magistrate of Anyang. His grandfather Fu rose no higher than recording secretary of Xing prefecture. His father was Si. Shangyin could already write essays as a boy. When Linghu Chu governed Heyang as military commissioner, Shangyin presented his writings to him, though he had not yet turned twenty. Chu admired his youth and talent, treated him with exceptional courtesy, and let him mingle with his sons. When Chu served at Tianping and Bian, Shangyin followed him as a staff officer. Chu paid his travel expenses each year and sent him to the capital with the tribute mission to sit for the examination. In 837 he finally passed the jinshi examination, took his first office as proofreader in the Secretariat, and was later transferred to magistrate of Hongnong. In 842 he again distinguished himself in the examination for legal and documentary excellence. When Wang Maoyuan governed Heyang, he recruited Shangyin as chief clerk and secured for him appointment as censor awaiting imperial disposition. Maoyuan admired his talent and gave him his daughter in marriage. Maoyuan had studied the classics and was a Confucian in learning, yet he came from a military family. Li Deyu had long favored him, and while Deyu held power he appointed him commander of Heyang. Deyu was locked in bitter enmity with Li Zongmin, Yang Sifu, and Linghu Chu. Once Shangyin entered Maoyuan's service, Zongmin's faction held him in deep contempt. By then Linghu Chu had died and his son Tao held an outer court post. Tao regarded Shangyin as ungrateful and especially despised his lack of principle. Before long Maoyuan died. Shangyin came to the capital in search of office but remained unemployed for a long time. Soon afterward Supervising Secretary Zheng Ya was sent to inspect Guizhou. He invited Shangyin to serve as administrative aide on the observation staff and acting vice director of the Ministry of Waterways. Early in the Dazhong reign Bai Minzhong came to power, with Linghu Tao in the inner secretariat; together they forced Li Deyu from office. Ya was condemned as a member of Deyu's faction and was demoted to prefect of Xunzhou. Shangyin followed Ya in the far south for several years. Three years later he returned to court. The capital intendant Lu Hongzheng memorialized to place him on his staff and put him in charge of petitions and memorials. The following year Linghu Tao became chief minister. Shangyin repeatedly petitioned to explain his circumstances, but Tao ignored him. When Hongzheng governed Xuzhou, Shangyin again served him as chief clerk. When that appointment ended he returned to court, again pressed his literary writings in search of office, and was appointed Erudite of the Imperial University. Soon the Henan intendant Liu Zhongying was sent to govern the eastern Shu region. He recruited Shangyin as administrative aide on his staff and acting director of the Ministry of Works. Late in the Dazhong reign Zhongying was demoted for an unauthorized execution. Shangyin was dismissed, returned to Zhengzhou, and died of illness not long afterward. Shangyin could write in the ancient prose style and disliked regulated parallel composition. He had served on Linghu Chu's staff. Chu excelled at memorials and edicts and taught Shangyin that craft, after which Shangyin began to write in the contemporary style of court documents. Learned and with a formidable memory, he wrote tirelessly once he took up the brush and was especially skilled at dirges and funeral offerings. His fame stood with Wen Tingyun of Taiyuan and Duan Chengshi of Nancheng; contemporaries called them the "Thirty-six." His literary sensibility was clear and refined, and in this he surpassed Tingyun. Yet both lacked firm moral principle. They relied on talent, behaved with eccentric vehemence, and men in power looked down on them. Neither advanced in official career and both were thwarted to the end of their lives. His younger brother Yishou also passed the jinshi examination and served repeatedly on provincial staffs. Shangyin left a collection of memorials and formal petitions in forty juan. Wen Tingyun came from Taiyuan. His original name was Qi, and his courtesy name was Feiqing. At the start of the Dazhong reign he sat for the jinshi examination, labored over his studies, and excelled above all in poetry and rhapsodies. When he first arrived in the capital, men of letters immediately held him in high regard. Yet his personal conduct was disorderly, he paid no heed to decorum, and he could set sensuous lyrics to the music of strings and pipes. He consorted with the dissolute sons of great families, such as Pei Cheng and Linghu Hao, gambling and drinking with them in drunken revelry all day long. Because of this he failed the examination year after year. When Xu Shang was stationed at Xiangyang, Tingyun went to join his staff and was appointed a touring officer. During the Xiantong reign, disheartened, he returned to the lower Yangzi region. Passing through Guangling, he nursed resentment that Linghu Tao, while in office, had not helped him win renown. Once there, he caroused wildly in the pleasure quarters with young upstarts, long neglected formal calls on officials, and even begged at Yangzi Courtyard. Drunk, he broke the night curfew, was beaten by the night watch, and returned with his face battered and teeth broken. The Yangzhou authorities brought suit. Linghu Tao had the night watch arrested and prosecuted, speaking at length of Tingyun's disreputable conduct in the pleasure quarters, and then released both parties. From then on his disreputable conduct became known throughout the capital. After reaching Chang'an, Tingyun wrote to high officials to clear his name. Xu Shang was then directing state affairs and spoke on his behalf with some effect. Before long Xu Shang was dismissed as chief minister and took up a post at Yangzhou. Shou grew angry with Tingyun, demoted him to magistrate of Fangcheng, later transferred him to magistrate of Sui county, where he died. His son Xian passed the jinshi examination. His younger brother Tinghao served on the staff at Xuzhou during the Xiantong reign. When the military governor Cui Yanlu was killed by Pang Xun, Tinghao was killed as well. Tingyun wrote a great deal, and the tonal craft of his poetry and rhapsodies was clear and refined. Men of letters praised him for it. Xue Feng, whose courtesy name was Taochen, came from Hedong. His father was Yi. Feng passed the jinshi at the start of the Huichang reign, received office, and entered service. When Cui, a proofreader in the Secretariat, was dismissed as chief minister and took up command at Hedzhong, he recruited Feng to his staff. When Xuan again took up chief ministerial duties, he memorialized to appoint Feng magistrate of Wannian and assign him to the Hall of Literature. Feng was later promoted repeatedly to supervising censor and then to a director in the Secretariat. Feng's writing was brilliant and his discourse sharp and impassioned. He prided himself on strategic talent, yet for years he failed to advance. While sitting for the jinshi examination he was especially close to Liu Cuan of Pengcheng. Cuan's literary skill did not match Feng's, and Feng often treated him with contempt. By the end of the Dazhong reign Cuan had risen to fame and served in the inner offices, while Feng grew ever more frustrated. From then on the two bore each other resentment. Before long Cuan took charge of state affairs. Someone recommended Feng for the post of drafter of edicts, but Cuan memorialized: "The former court established that appointees to the drafting and secretariat posts of the Two Departments must first serve in prefectural and county office. Feng has never governed a commandery and should first be tested in such a post." Feng was then sent out as prefect of Bazhou. Before long Shen Xun, Yang Shou, and Wang Duo rose from the Hanlin Academy to become chief ministers and generals in succession. All were jinshi of the same year as Feng, yet his literary talent was the finest. After Yang Shou became chief minister, Feng wrote a poem that ran: "One must know the courtier bearing the golden seal who faces the Son of Heaven. Both alike are passers-by sidestepping the road along the sand embankment. A majestic phoenix appearing at the right moment is hailed as an auspicious sage; a hidden dragon without water vainly claims communion with the divine." When Shou heard of it, he was deeply offended. Feng was again sent out as prefect of Pengzhou. When Shou was dismissed as chief minister, Feng entered court as vice director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices and drafting reviewer. When Wang Duo became chief minister, Feng wrote another poem: "Yesterday a goose feather weighed ten thousand jun; today mountains and peaks are lighter than a speck of dust." Duo again resented him. Because Feng relied on his talent and was narrow and quick to take offense, men of standing despised him. He was promoted to director of the Secretariat and died. His son Tinggui passed the jinshi examination during the Zhonghe reign. At the start of the Datong reign he rose through several posts to vice director in the Ministry of Honors, was formally appointed drafter of edicts, and was invested as secretariat drafter. In 896 he was sent on mission to Taiyuan. On reporting back that Emperor Zhaozong had moved to Huazhou, he was appointed left regular attendant. He pleaded illness, resigned from office, and traveled as a guest in Chengdu. During the Guanghua reign he again became secretariat drafter, was promoted to vice minister of both Justice and Personnel, served as acting director of the civil examinations in the Ministry of Rites, and was appointed left vice director of the Secretariat. After entering the service of Later Liang, he rose to minister of rites. Li Zheng, whose courtesy name was Changshi, came from Longxi. In 871 he passed the jinshi examination. During the Qianfu reign he served repeatedly on provincial staffs. During Huang Chao's rebellion he took refuge at Pingyang. When Emperor Xizong returned to the capital, Zheng was summoned and appointed a director in the Secretariat, then promoted to director in the Ministry of Honors and made drafter of edicts. When Emperor Xizong again moved to Baoji, Zheng was unable to accompany him. At Fengxiang the Prince of Xiang usurped an imperial title and forced Zheng to serve as a Hanlin academician. Having been tainted by service under the usurping regime, he could not rest easy in his mind. Later Zhu Mei seized power. The hundred officials fell into disorder, and court institutions sank into chaos. Once, after court was dismissed, Zheng halted his horse at the Gate of the Nation, gazed toward the southern mountains, and recited: "After court at Zichen ends, paired mandarin ducks are strung together; before the Crimson Phoenix Tower I halt my horse to look. Only the color of Mount Zhongnan remains, clear and bright as ever, filling Chang'an." When he finished reciting, tears streamed down his face. When Wang Xingyu killed Zhu Mei, the Prince of Xiang fled. The capital fell into chaos, and Zheng was killed by mutinous troops. His wife, Lady Lu, was learned, could write, and was beautiful. After Zheng died she lay over his corpse wailing. When bandits pressed her, she kept weeping and would not move. They threatened her with weapons and even severed one of her arms, yet she never turned away and was killed by the bandits. All who heard of it mourned her. Li Juchuan, whose courtesy name was Xiayi, came from Longyou. He was a descendant of Li Daoxuan of the founding eighteen scholars and a grandnephew of Li Fengji. His father Xun passed the jinshi examination in 854. Juchuan sat for the jinshi during the Qianfu reign. As the realm fell into great disorder and he wandered in exile, eager for salary and rank, he turned to the pen and entered the staffs of regional lords. When Wang Chongrong was stationed at Hedzhong, he recruited Juchuan as chief secretary. At that time the emperor was in Shu, rebels held the capital, and Chongrong rallied the regional lords to join forces against the bandits. Military dispatches and memorials piled on his desk until they overflowed. Juchuan wrote with swift brilliance, his brush flying across the page. When his dispatches reached neighboring regions, all were stirred. Chongrong's success in recovery owed much to Juchuan's help. When Chongrong was killed by his subordinates, court opinion blamed his staff, and Juchuan was demoted to an aide in Hanzhong. At that time Yang Shouliang commanded Xingyuan and knew Juchuan of old. When he heard Juchuan had arrived, he said joyfully to a guest: "Heaven has sent Secretary Li to me!" [Close quotation.] He immediately appointed Juchuan to manage the secretariat and promoted him through several staff posts. During the Jingfu reign Shouliang was attacked by Li Maozhen. When the city fell, he set out with several hundred followers intending to go over to Taiyuan. Entering Qin, he was captured by Han Jian's army at Hua. Juchuan was then with Shouliang and was shackled as well. On the road Juchuan inscribed a poem on a tree leaf and sent it to Han Jian, commander of Hua. The verse was mournful and moving, and Jian gladly released him from his bonds. After Shouliang was executed, Jian immediately appointed Juchuan chief secretary. Before long Li Maozhen invaded the capital, and the emperor halted at Hua. Han Jian, with the resources of a single province, had to supply the imperial court and feared he could not manage it. He sent Juchuan to circulate a proclamation throughout the realm requesting aid in transporting provisions, so that all might jointly restore the royal house and rebuild the capital. Dispatches and replies poured in from every direction. Juchuan drafted responses with fluent prose and satisfying logic. Emperor Zhaozong held him in deep esteem, and Juchuan's name at once spread throughout the realm. When Emperor Zhaozong returned to the capital, Juchuan was specially appointed remonstrance grandee and remained to assist Han Jian. At the start of the Guanghua reign Zhu Quanzhong captured Hedzhong and advanced into Tong Pass. Jian was afraid and sent Juchuan to see Zhu Quanzhong and offer submission. Arriving at Hedzhong, Juchuan spoke calmly of the situation. Juchuan laid out the advantages and dangers of the situation. Zhu Quanzhong was then plotting to seize the throne, and when he heard Juchuan's analysis he took offense. The aide Jing Xiang, also valued by Zhu Quanzhong for his literary skill, feared that keeping Juchuan would diminish his own standing and said to Quanzhong: "Remonstrance Grandee Li's writing is indeed fine, but it does not serve his master well." [Close quotation.] That same day Juchuan was killed by Zhu Quanzhong. Sikong Tu, whose courtesy name was Biaosheng, was originally from Linzi. His great-grandfather Sui served as magistrate of Mi. His grandfather Luan served as director in the Ministry of Works. His father Yu was skilled in administrative methods. At the start of the Dazhong reign Vice Minister of Revenue Lu Hongzheng oversaw the salt and iron monopoly and memorialized to appoint Yu commissioner of the Anyi two-pool salt monopoly and acting director in the Ministry of Rites. Previously the salt laws were loosely defined, and officials often violated the regulations; Yu then drafted ten articles of new regulations and memorialized them. To this day they are regarded as convenient. He entered court service as vice director in the Ministry of Justice, was promoted to director in the Ministry of Revenue, and died. Tu passed the jinshi examination in 869. The chief examiner Wang Ning regarded him as especially remarkable among the successful candidates. When Ning was demoted to prefect of Shangzhou, Tu asked to accompany him. Ning valued him all the more, and when Ning was assigned to inspect Xuancheng and Shezhou he recruited Tu as chief guest. He was summoned and appointed palace censor. Because he was slow in reaching court he was demoted to registrar in the Court of Imperial Entertainments and assigned to the eastern capital branch. In 879 Chief Minister Lu Xie was dismissed and served as a guest at the eastern capital branch. Tu kept company with him. Xie admired Tu's lofty integrity and treated him with generous courtesy. Once, visiting Tu's house, he wrote on the wall by hand: "The surname Sikong is noble; the rank of censor is low. If this old man were still in office, you need not brood over hardship and obscurity." The next year Xie returned to court. Passing through Shanzhou and Guozhou he said to the Shan commander Lu Wo: "Censor Sikong is a man of lofty character. You should treat him generously." Wo that same day memorialized to appoint Tu to his staff. That year Xie again took charge of state affairs, summoned Tu as vice director in the Ministry of Rites, granted him the crimson robe and fish bag, and promoted him to director in that ministry. That winter Huang Chao's rebels invaded the capital. The emperor fled, Tu was unable to accompany him, and withdrew to Hedzhong. At that time the former chief minister Wang Hui was also at Pu and treated Tu with great generosity. Several years later Hui received orders to take command at Lu and memorialized to appoint Tu his deputy. Hui never took up the post, and the appointment came to nothing. When Emperor Xizong returned from Shu and halted at Fengxiang, Tu was summoned to draft edicts and soon formally appointed secretariat drafter. That year Emperor Xizong moved to Baoji. Tu again could not accompany him and withdrew to Hedzhong. At the start of the Longji reign he was again summoned and appointed secretariat drafter. Before long he again pleaded illness and resigned. When Hebei fell into disorder, he took up residence at Huayin. During the Jingfu reign he was again summoned as remonstrance grandee. At that time the court was weak and institutions were in ruins. Tu deeply felt that leaving retirement was worse than remaining in seclusion, pleaded illness, and refused to take office. During the Qianning reign he was again summoned as vice minister of revenue. He came once to court to offer thanks, but within days begged to return to the mountains and was permitted to do so. When Emperor Zhaozong was at Hua, Tu was summoned and appointed vice minister of war. He claimed a foot ailment that prevented him from performing court bows and merely sent a memorial of thanks. When Emperor Zhaozong moved to Luoyang, Zhu Quanzhong sought to bring him under Liang control. Liu Can curried the usurper's favor, framed members of the old elite, and an edict summoned Tu to court. Tu feared execution, forced himself through illness to reach Luoyang, and on the day of audience dropped his court tablet and lost all decorum. His manner was utterly uncouth. Can knew he could not be bent and issued an edict saying: "Sikong Tu, outstanding in talent, passed the examination and entered the ranks of high office. Having cultivated loftiness to disdain the age, he is like one who moved a mountain to fish for fame. His heart delights only in living as a recluse by flowing streams; office is not his sole pursuit of salary and sustenance. Neither suitable for barbarian lands nor for a benevolent court, he is ill suited to a government of impartial justice; Upon further reflection, he should be allowed to follow his resolve to live in rustic seclusion. He is permitted to return to the mountains." Tu had an ancestral villa in Wangguan Valley in the Zhongtiao Mountains, with springs, rocks, woods, and pavilions well suited to secluded living. From then on he lived in lofty seclusion at Kaopan, daily roaming and composing poetry there with eminent monks and reclusive scholars. In his later writing he especially cultivated free unrestraint. Once, modeling Bai Juyi's Biography of the Drunken Chanter, he wrote Record of the Rest-Rest Pavilion: "The Sikong family's Rest-Rest Pavilion at Zhenyi Stream was originally named Wash-the-Tassel Pavilion and was burned by the Shan army." In the guihai year of Tianfu it was rebuilt amid ruined walls, and its name was changed to Rest-Rest. Rest means repose, and also beauty; in repose, full beauty remains. Broadly speaking: measured by talent, he ought first to rest; measured by allotted fate, he ought second to rest; old and deaf, he ought third to rest. Moreover, idle in youth, unrestrained in maturity, and obstinate in old age—these three qualities are none of them useful for aiding the age, and so again he ought to rest. Still he worried that in troubled times he could not trust himself. Then he napped by day and met two monks who said to him: "We were once your teachers. You once strained after the Way, sharp yet not steadfast, bound by profit and desire. Fortunately you awakened and repented, and will again follow us at this stream. Moreover, though you have withdrawn, you have also been envied by wicked men. You should endure insult and keep yourself warned, so as to preserve your integrity from beginning to end and rank your standing with Tao Yuanming and Bai Juyi a thousand years hence. What more could you seek!" He therefore composed the Song of the Endurance-of-Insult Recluse and inscribed it on the northeast pillar: "Tut-tut! Rest, rest, rest; no, no, no. Though tricks are many, nature and spirit are base; luckily one is long taught to dwell in leisure. Rest, rest, rest; no, no, no. One game of chess, one brazier of medicine—the intent of heaven and the mood of the age can be gauged. The white sun especially urges the merry man onward; gold cannot buy the privilege of riding a crane to immortality. If one says: 'What can you do?' The answer is: 'Endure insult—that is all.'" His eccentric vehemence, whistling defiance, and proud disdain were mostly of this kind. After Tu escaped Liu Can's peril and returned to the mountains, he prepared his tomb and final arrangements in advance. When old friends came, he led them into the burial chamber to compose poetry and drink together. Some showed discomfort, and Tu admonished them, saying: "The man of attainment takes the great view. Dark and bright are one, and this is not merely a brief visit here. Why do you not broaden your view!" [Close quotation.] Tu wore plain cloth and carried a dove-tailed staff. When he went out he was accompanied by the female household member Luantai. At seasonal village rites, rain prayers, sacrifices, and drum-and-dance gatherings, Tu always attended and sat with rustic elders, never showing arrogance. Wang Chongrong and his family especially valued him. Seasonal offerings and gifts never ceased on the road to his door. In the year after the Tang dynasty fell, hearing that Prince Hui had been assassinated at Jiyin, he fell into displeasure and illness. Within days he died, at the age of seventy-two. He left collected writings in thirty juan. Tu had no son and took his nephew He as his heir. He rose to prefect of Yongzhou. Because he had taken a nephew as heir, he was once impeached by a censor, but Emperor Zhaozong did not hold him accountable. The eulogy says: The splendor of the state lies in the forming and completion of human culture. At intervals ages produce outstanding men who stir literary ornament and unfold brilliance. Like swift Qiji they stride in excellence; like Xian and Shao they sound the correct music. Their brilliance flows through silk and plain scrolls, looking down even upon the ages of Ji and Ying.
